‘Hobbit’ hominins scavenged meat left over by Komodo dragons

New Scientist July 03, 2026

3 July 2026

The diminutive ancient humans nicknamed hobbits that lived on the Indonesian island of Flores until around 50,000 years ago had limited hunting skills, according to a study of animal bones found in their caves. Instead, researchers think they scavenged meat that was left behind by Komodo dragons.

Fossils of Homo floresiensis were first announced to the world in 2004. These humans stood just over a metre tall and their remains have been dated to between 90,000 and 50,000 years old.

Based on stone tools and blackened bones found alongside their remains, it was initially thought they were capable of advanced behaviour such as the controlled use of fire and ability to hunt the largest animals on their island. But in recent years, the cognitive abilities of these small-brained hominins have been a matter of debate.

“I would argue that our field at large still holds on to this idea that Homo floresiensis had to have some form of advanced cognition to have reached the island and survived in a depauperate faunal community, regardless of brain size,” says Elizabeth Veatch at the Smithsonian Institution in Washington DC.

The Liang Bua cave where the remains of H. floresiensis were found contains many bones of a dwarf elephant species (Stegodon florensis insularis). But Veatch and her colleagues suspected that these animals had been killed by Komodo dragons, one of the world’s largest reptiles, which live on Flores and some other Indonesian islands.

To determine exactly what kind of marks Komodo dragons leave on the bones of large mammals that they eat, Veatch and her team fed a dead goat to one of the giant reptiles at Zoo Atlanta in Georgia. “Stegodon are extinct and it would be near impossible to create an experiment where a Komodo dragon was fed a whole elephant,” says Veatch.

After the Komodo had finished its meal, 72 bones remained, 26 of which had a total of 192 toothmarks. The researchers then compared these bones to over 3000 Stegodon bone fragments found in deposits in Liang Bua cave associated only with H. floresiensis, as well as nearly 7000 much more recent bones from giant rats that were associated with Homo sapiens at the same cave. They also examined each of these roughly 10,000 bones for signs of having been exposed to fire.

They found that in their experiment with the goat, the Komodo dragon favoured the parts of the carcass that had the most meat, such as the hindquarters and forequarters.

However, the cut marks left by H. floresiensis’s stone tools on the Stegodon bones were primarily on the less desirable cuts such as cranial bones and thoracic vertebrae – an unexpected result if humans had first access to the dead elephants.

Out of the more than 3000 Stegodon bone remains associated with the small ancient humans, only one had any sign of being exposed to fire, and that was most likely from a section of the deposit that was disturbed and heated by later humans. By contrast, a fifth of all the rat bone remains left by modern humans after the hobbits became extinct showed signs of being cooked.

“The rat bones demonstrate the pattern clearly – zero burned bones in Homo floresiensis layers, hundreds burned in modern human layers,” says Veatch. “Claims of advanced behaviour have been slowly chipped away, but our study directly confirms our suspicion that Homo floresiensis did not use fire or hunt big game as was originally claimed.”

Adam Brumm at Griffith University in Brisbane, Australia says the study shows “convincingly” that Homo floresiensis probably did not hunt Stegodon but rather scavenged their remains.

Martin Porr at the University of Western Australia says previous claims of Stegodon hunting and fire use have been controversial. “In a sense, the new findings bring Homo floresiensis more in line with what we know about other small-bodied hominins, such as Australopithecines, and this would make some sense given their brain capacity and body weight,” says Porr.

But other small hominins have been found only in Africa. The big question is whether Homo floresiensis is descended from small hominins that had a much wider range than we thought, or whether it is descended from larger hominins like Homo erectus, which subsequently got smaller and lost certain abilities.

“I think that both options remain possible right now and it will require more research on and around Flores to clarify this,” says Porr.

Journal reference:

Science Advances DOI: 10.1126/sciadv. aeb7219

A volcano has erupted remnants of Earth's primordial magma ocean

New Scientist July 03, 2026

3 July 2026

A rising underwater volcano off the coast of Madagascar has been spewing up chemical traces of material from a primordial magma ocean in the first 100 million years of Earth’s history.

Scientists generally suspect that Earth’s mantle – the thick layer of hot rock beneath the crust – has been steadily churning for more than 4 billion years, gradually erasing most chemical traces of the planet’s earliest history.

“This is going to change a lot of things [in earth science], because now we have proof that materials dating back 4.5 billion years – from the very beginning of Earth’s history – still exist in sufficient quantities to be sampled in a volcano,” says Catherine Chauvel at the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) in Paris.

During the Hadean eon, a Mars-sized object collided with Earth, breaking off debris that scientists believe later formed the moon. The impact heated the young planet so intensely that it became covered by a global magma ocean. Over the next few million years, the molten rock cooled and crystallised, and the earliest crust began to form above the mantle.

Some scientists suspected that traces of this primordial crystallisation survived in Earth’s mantle, but they lacked the analytical precision to prove it, says Chauvel.

In May 2018, an unusual swarm of earthquakes off the French island of Mayotte, between Madagascar and Mozambique, led scientists to discover a new volcano about 50 kilometres further east, named Fani Maoré. Eruptions over the following three years drained so much magma from underneath Mayotte that it sank about 20 centimetres.

Chauvel and her colleagues recovered volcanic rock samples from Fani Maoré and nearby Mayotte to compare the chemistry of the new volcano with that of the older volcanic system. They teamed up with Claudine Israel at the University of Cambridge to investigate further, using a newly developed ultra-precise technique to measure tiny differences in neodymium isotopes. Such isotopes preserve a chemical record of how Earth’s primordial magma ocean crystallised as the young planet cooled, says Israel.

The team found that, compared to Mayotte’s lava, the Fani Maoré lava had a slightly higher ratio of neodymium-142 to neodymium-144. That higher ratio probably reflects a pocket of ancient mantle that escaped billions of years of mixing and is still relatively rich in bridgmanite – a mineral thought to have been among the first to crystallise from Earth’s primordial magma ocean.

“It’s always exciting to find something you’ve been looking for – and that nobody else has found yet,” says Chauvel.

The findings suggest Earth’s mantle might never have become as thoroughly mixed as many geologists had assumed. That could help scientists reconstruct how Earth’s primordial magma ocean solidified, says Israel.

“For the first time, we’ve shown experimentally how the mantle crystallised from the magma ocean, and how that crystallisation created chemical heterogeneity from the very beginning,” she says.

The new findings provide plausible evidence that Earth’s mantle still preserves extremely ancient material, says Tim Johnson at Curtin University in Perth, Australia. “This seems to be an exciting advance,” he says.

“It takes an enormous amount of work to get a technique like that working properly, and it looks like they’ve succeeded,” says Bernard Bourdon at the CNRS in Lyon.

The study offers an unprecedented glimpse into a period of Earth’s history for which almost no direct evidence survives, he adds. “It’s a bit like discovering a sample of Earth’s core that somehow made it all the way to the surface,” says Bourdon.

For Richard Carlson at Carnegie Science in Washington, D. C., the precision alone is noteworthy. “Anyone who has experience with these measurements would recognise it as a major achievement,” he says.

Journal reference:

Nature DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-10719-w

Audacious mission to rescue NASA's falling telescope has launched

New Scientist July 03, 2026

3 July 2026

One of NASA’s premier space telescopes is falling, and an audacious mission to rescue it has just begun. The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is months from dropping back to Earth, but if the rescue works, it could continue watching the sky for years to come.

All satellites’ orbits eventually decay, and Swift is no exception. The outer edges of Earth’s atmosphere have been dragging it down since it launched in 2004: its initial orbit was at an altitude of about 600 kilometres from the ground, and now it’s only about 375 kilometres up. Its descent in recent years was faster than expected because of powerful solar flares depositing energy into the atmosphere, puffing it outwards and increasing drag on satellites.

So if NASA wanted to keep Swift operating, the agency had few options. The one that won out was a proposal by Katalyst Space Technologies, a small start-up based in Arizona, to give the orbiting observatory a boost.

The plan rests on a satellite called LINK, designed to grab Swift with a trio of robotic arms and pull it upward. At less than 2 metres tall, its main body is only about one-third the size of Swift, but it is flanked by immense sheets of solar panels to power its thrusters and grappling arms.

LINK launched atop a Northrop Grumman Pegasus XL rocket on the morning of 3 July, in what is intended to be the final launch for Pegasus XL before it is retired. The spacecraft will now go through a few weeks of testing in space before it grabs Swift and slowly pushes upwards for about two months, letting go when it reaches its original 600-kilometre altitude. If all goes well, this manoeuvre will keep Swift operating for as much as a decade longer.

Swift was originally built to study gamma-ray bursts, which are the brightest and most powerful explosions in the universe. Over the years, it has detected about 1800 of these blasts, and has also made crucial discoveries about other cosmic objects, ranging from comets and planets to supernovae and black holes.

Boosting it will allow it to continue observing, but if it works, it will also be an important demonstration that it is possible to save a space telescope. “Swift wasn’t designed to be serviced,” said Ghonhee Lee, CEO of Katalyst, in a statement. “By demonstrating we can quickly and cost-effectively extend its lifetime, we’re creating a blueprint for servicing spacecraft that were never designed for on-orbit maintenance.” This could be a cost-effective way to extend the lifetimes of other satellites as well, in particular the Hubble Space Telescope, which is predicted to fall in the 2030s if it doesn’t get a boost.

Orangutan mothers seem to plan playdates for their offspring

New Scientist July 03, 2026

3 July 2026

Orangutan mothers seem to make trips into the territories of other mothers with similarly aged offspring so the youngsters can play together.

Play is essential to how many animals learn, strengthening social and motor skills, and teaching crucial behaviour. Yet orangutans are a solitary species, and mothers give birth to a single infant, which they raise alone for six to seven years. The young socialise together when they get the chance, but how often this happens and how it comes about are poorly understood.

“I think the assumption would be that orangutans require less play because they’re less social than the other apes, but orangutan males have to fight, so they have to practise that somewhere,” says Zarin Machanda at Tufts University in Massachusetts.

To dig into this, Odd Jacobson at the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior in Konstanz, Germany, and his colleagues have looked at 15 years’ worth of data on 31 wild Bornean orangutan (Pongo pygmaeus wurmbii) mother-offspring pairs. The data covers about 30,000 hours of observations that reveal where the animals were, whom they were with and what they were doing.

The team found that mothers with similarly aged offspring spent a disproportionately high amount of time together in the same area. Youngsters tended to play in these situations, and play was more likely if the mothers were closely related.

The distance the apes travelled increased in the days before and after the playdate, as the mothers headed into the neighbour’s territory and then home afterwards.

“Our study provides strong evidence that wild Bornean orangutan mothers adjust their ranging behavior to increase their offspring’s access to social play,” write Jacobson and his colleagues, who didn’t respond to New Scientist’s request for comment.

It is possible the young apes are just playing where orangutans have gathered near a plentiful supply of fruit, much like brown bear cubs have been seen playing together when their mothers converge on a river full of salmon. But the meet-ups happened regardless of how much fruit was available in the area, and the researchers found that the increased travelling meant less time feeding. This led them to suggest that these encounters are planned at a cost to the mothers’ own foraging, rather than being part of it.

It is almost impossible to determine intentionality with behavioural data like this, says Machanda, but she says “it’s possible that there’s something different about the way that mothers play with their babies and peers play, and they’re making a choice to get their babies socialised with peers”.

Adriano Lameira at the University of Warwick, UK, says the findings are in line with what we know about the huge investment orangutans make in raising their offspring and their cognitive capabilities.

He doesn’t think orangutan mothers call ahead to arrange playdates, though. Male orangutans use long calls to communicate their travel direction a day in advance, he says, but females aren’t thought to use long-distance calls for social coordination.

He thinks the meet-ups come down to what the orangutans can hear and see from the trees, their local knowledge – such as which trees are fruiting or where there are big lianas for youngsters to climb – and their ability to understand what others would do.

“One mother will likely be able to estimate, based on the other mother’s last location and typical range, which resources they will be searching for and where they will most likely be,” says Lameira.

Reference:

bioRxiv DOI: 10.64898/2026.06.20.733430

Evocative photos of Canadian Arctic win New Scientist Editors Award

New Scientist July 03, 2026

3 July 2026

The realities of a changing global climate collide with years of tradition in Natalya Saprunova’s icy blue photograph, above, part of a series that won the New Scientist Editors Award in the Earth Photo 2026 competition.

The image shows a hunter from an Inuit community in Tuktoyaktuk on Canada’s Arctic coast holding a goose decoy meant to lure migrating birds. In the background, a pale sky touches banks of melting ice and murky water already studded with several faux birds. Indigenous peoples in the region used to make these decoys from reeds, but it isn’t just the materials they work with that have now changed – rising temperatures have affected the actual birds, shifting their migratory patterns and making them harder to hunt. Saprunova documents this and other related changes in her winning series, focusing especially on the melting permafrost.

Below, an Inuit resident of Victoria Island handles fish, another essential resource for the local community, and another animal whose behaviour has changed with the changing climate. Because permafrost thawing accelerates coastal erosion, it also introduces harmful compounds like mercury into the habitats of commonly eaten fish, endangering food supplies.

Taking a wider view in the image below, Saprunova captures the texture of changes to the Arctic landscape itself, a web of sunken polygons filled with water and occasionally studded with conical, ice-cored hills. As permafrost melts, the land becomes uneven and makes it harder for animals like caribou to traverse their home. “The thaw is not just melting ice, it is reshaping the map upon which animals and people have always relied,” writes Saprunova in her submission for the prize.

The situation is even more dire when she photographs the hamlet of Sachs Harbour where whole cliffs of permafrost are disappearing. A rugged, uneven cliff laced with cracks is shown dangerously close to homes, below. The contrast between these neat residences and the eroding land conveys the urgency of climate catastrophe in the Arctic. Canada has the longest inhabited Arctic coastline in the world and some of its inhabitants stand the grim chance of becoming the country’s first climate refugees.

Accordingly, Saprunova photographs Pelly Island, below, which is known to be disappearing. The permafrost that once comprised it is now melting away and releasing greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, which could, devastatingly, speed up both the rise in global temperatures and the further melting of the island. A cliff of black rock looks monstrously barren, as a nearby tiny human figure looks at the water. Exposed veins of gray and white rock only underline how much climate change is wounding their world.

Images from this series will be shown at an exhibition at the Royal Geographical Society in London until 24 July.

Northland meth crisis deepens as families fight to break cycle of control

New Zealand Herald July 10, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Grandmothers dealing meth and single mothers being recruited to sell it were once unthinkable in Northland. Today, community leaders say such stories show methamphetamine’s grip on the region, with dealers exploiting addiction to control vulnerable people and draw them deeper into the drug trade. Brodie Stone reports.

“All you need to do is feed someone for a little while until they’ve got the hunger for it, and then you’ve got the control,” Ōtangarei Trust chief executive Martin Kaipo said.

He knew of grandmothers dealing meth and some mothers so consumed by addiction that they no longer knew their children.

Kaipo said meth dealers used the drug to get people hooked and working for them.

Those pulling the strings were ruthless, he said, making it hard for families to help relatives escape their role as drug mules.

“Once you’re addicted and hooked into it, you either belong to someone or you are the man.”

Kaipo said methamphetamine dealers had moved from cities into remote areas near the coast or in the countryside.

He believed they targeted vulnerable communities because they saw them as easy places to make money.

Last month, a police operation uncovered what Kaipo described. Police alleged methamphetamine was being manufactured in homes across isolated Far North communities, with single mothers allegedly being drawn into dealing after becoming addicted themselves.

Kaipo said the harm from meth addiction had a ripple effect.

“You’re sacrificing family, and you don’t even know that you’re doing it.”

Kaipo believed family could be the answer. He said he had seen “tremendous results” from whānau who took a no-frills approach to helping loved ones through addiction at home.

“I think the war on drugs is not necessarily the war we should be fighting. We should be dealing with the addiction,” he said.

“You’ve got to look at the family, where the strengths are within the families, where the leadership is. And it really takes community to fight that war.”

The recruitment of vulnerable people into dealing was something Kaikohe’s Whakaoranga Whānau Recovery Hub (WOW Hub) chief executive Rhonda Zielinski said she saw reflected in her work.

“You know, it’s no different from the people in the supermarkets that give out free chocolates or taste this, taste that. It’s a marketing strategy.”

Zielinski believed Northland was a hotspot for meth use because vulnerable communities were an easy target.

“If we didn’t have people who were poor and traumatised and didn’t have all that stuff to deal with, then maybe the demand for drugs would decrease.”

Her concerns were reflected in wastewater testing from the first quarter, which showed Northland continued to have the highest per-capita daily methamphetamine consumption in the country and remained above its previous four-quarter average.

Zielinski described her work as being “in the trenches” with those battling addiction.

“We need to be there because when we change one adult, we change a whole family, and that changes a whole bloodline.”

Zielinski said methamphetamine affected people’s wairua.

“Once you start taking meth, it actually robs your soul.”

However, she urged people not to judge those struggling with addiction as they were often using drugs to cope with trauma.

Zielinski said recovery was possible and could have a generational impact.

She felt the Government was so busy “whipping from the top” that it risked overlooking people who needed support to overcome addiction.

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith disagreed.

He pointed to the meth action plan announced last November, which included $30 million over four years to increase services available to communities hardest hit.

Maritime operations to disrupt organised crime networks in the Pacific, increasing police enforcement, and strengthening border security were also announced.

Goldsmith said drug harm was an “extremely difficult” issue and the Government was working hard to turn it around.

“We’re monitoring progress closely, but we know it will take time to see consistent results.”

The scale of the problem was reflected in wastewater testing, which showed methamphetamine consumption nearly doubled in the last quarter of 2024. High availability and lower prices had “almost certainly” contributed to increased demand countrywide, according to last year’s Drugs in Wastewater Testing annual overview.

Methamphetamine use had remained at that elevated level and ticked up again this year, according to Massey University Professor Chris Wilkins, from the Shore & Whāriki Drug Research Team.

He said the cost of meth had fallen as well.

“We’re in a pretty extraordinary situation where the price of meth is now ... in a similar bracket, broadly speaking, to cannabis.”

Wilkins said the methamphetamine market had changed since he began researching it more than two decades ago. Seizures that once attracted attention because they involved tens of kilograms had been eclipsed by routine interceptions of hundreds of kilograms.

Northland was the site of New Zealand’s largest methamphetamine bust in 2016, involving almost 500kg of meth, but that mark was overtaken by a 747kg haul in Auckland in March 2023.

Northland’s geography made it well suited to drug smuggling, Wilkins said, with the region’s 3200km coastline providing ample opportunities to bring contraband ashore.

Evidence suggested Mexican cartels had established reliable supply routes, he said.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon recently identified methamphetamine as a key challenge, saying drugs were reaching New Zealand via Pacific trafficking routes. He made the comments while at a Mayoral Inner City Taskforce meeting in Whangārei on Tuesday.

He said the Government was working with international partners to disrupt supply chains before drugs reached New Zealand, while also focusing on improving addiction treatment services and identifying programmes that delivered results.

Northland District Commander Superintendent Matthew Srhoj agreed methamphetamine was an issue, especially in the Far North.

“We all do have to do our part. There has been a slight lack of co-ordination around the services and there’s probably not enough services ... but I think we’re getting better at co-ordinating work and other initiatives are starting to have some impact now.”

Brodie Stone covers crime and emergency for the Northern Advocate. She has spent most of her life in Whangārei and is passionate about delving into issues that matter to Northlanders and beyond.

Disputes Tribunal orders ex to return $24k after partner’s spend on home renovation, boat expenses

New Zealand Herald July 10, 2026

Items bought for the man's home renovation project showed up on the woman's credit card invoices. The Disputes Tribunal has ordered him to pay back the money. Photo / 123rf

A woman used settlement money from a previous relationship to support her new partner’s home renovation project and his boating interests.

When the brief relationship ended, Nicola* asked for the money back.

But Ken* believed her contributions were a gift which he never asked for.

Nicola said Ken knew she had received money from her relationship property settlement and shortly after requested financial help with the renovations to his house.

Now, her claim for $29,000 in the Disputes Tribunal has been partially upheld, with an order he return just under $24,000.

Tribunal referee Shelley Munro said the evidence supported Nicola’s claim that the money would be repaid if the relationship ended.

According to a recently released decision, the couple were in a brief relationship from late 2023 until March 2024.

Ken was completing significant renovations to his property when the relationship began, Munro said in the tribunal decision.

Nicola had recently received a payout from a previous relationship property settlement.

She transferred “large sums of money” to Ken and paid for renovation items based on what she described as an agreement between them that he would repay the amounts if the relationship did not work out.

If it did, she could live rent-free in the house with her children.

Between October 2023 and February 2024, a “significant number of transactions were made”, including payments on Nicola’s credit card for items at two hardware stores.

Munro said these were consistent with products for building, including the purchase of a $3000 oven.

Ken said Nicola did not have to buy it, but chose to do so. He also said Nicola decided to buy the oven for when she and her children moved in.

“This, of course, did not happen,” Munro said.

Ken also spent nearly $2000 of Nicola’s money on a navigation system for his boat and a further $3496 on servicing the boat and installing the system.

He claimed it was an “early Christmas present”, which he neither asked for nor agreed to repay.

Nicola said she would never spend so much on a Christmas present.

Munro said over the same period there were 15 separate bank transfers to Ken, ranging from $100 to $5000, totalling $11,693 and 18 credit card transactions Nicola claimed were for items she paid on behalf of Ken and he was to reimburse her under the loan agreement.

Munro had to assess the terms of the alleged loan agreement.

If it was a loan, she had to determine whether it had been breached by not being repaid and, if so, the amount of any proven loss.

Ken disputed that there was any agreement requiring him to repay the money.

He said Nicola had received the money from her settlement and was “spending constantly”.

Ken said he never asked her to pay for things or transfer money to him and therefore it was not a loan.

He said he often bought her things like “lunch and smokes”, and she would transfer money to him.

Ken also claimed he looked after her children while she worked and that the money she gave him helped pay for groceries and the “many holidays” when they went jetboating.

Nicola disagreed.

She said her children attended school and preschool and did not need looking after. She submitted bank statements showing the money she spent on holidays and boating with Ken which she was not seeking to recover.

Nicola stated that the terms of the agreement were clear.

Contact the Open Justice team

Munro said based on the large number of transactions she did not accept Ken’s evidence that she “just did it and sometimes he didn’t know”.

“Having considered the evidence, I accept that there was an agreement for [Nicola] to advance money to [Ken] and that this would be repaid if the relationship ended,” Munro said.

She noted the relationship was only a few months old when the large payments were made.

“It makes no sense to suggest [Nicola] would do this or buy him such large items for the house,” Munro said.

Nor did Munro accept Ken’s explanation that he “did not know” Nicola was making the direct bank transfers, or that some of them were repayments for smokes, milk, childcare or contributions to groceries and holidays.

She found the transfers were advances made directly to Ken by way of a loan he had requested and which were subsequently documented to calculate what was owing.

Regarding the credit card payments, Munro found some related to the installation of products in Ken’s home were proven, but she was not satisfied that others fell within the loan agreement.

Nor was it clear those items were specifically for Ken.

Nicola’s claim also included $3500 for mileage on a vehicle Ken borrowed from her, but that part of the claim was dismissed.

Munro said there was insufficient evidence to show the date when Ken started using the vehicle.

She said the tribunal had jurisdiction to hear the claim because it concerned a contract rather than a claim under the Property Relationships Act.

“That is because of the very brief relationship and the fact that the claim is one in contract – that the parties entered into an agreement for money to be loaned with the intention of repayment,” she said.

*Names have been anonymised in keeping with Disputes Tribunal rules around name suppression.

Tracy Neal is a Nelson-based Open Justice reporter at NZME. She was previously RNZ’s regional reporter in Nelson-Marlborough and has covered general news, including court and local government for the Nelson Mail.

Thousands are expected to pack Auckland’s Spark Arena for a landmark celebration during Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s whirlwind 24-hour visit to New Zealand.

Modi, who is one of the world’s most high-profile leaders, arrived at Auckland Airport late last night before his action-packed day today.

His arrival drew a crowd of supporters, despite the “well-advanced” security operation planned with specialist police staff flown in from around the country.

The 75-year-old exchanged a welcome hug with Prime Minister Christopher Luxon last night before he was expected to mark New Zealand’s recently signed free trade agreement with India during his visit today.

Luxon said Modi was also interested in New Zealand’s high-tech and high-performance sport approach.

Contact the New Zealand Herald newsroom

Luxon earlier told Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast that Modi’s first visit would be a “historic event”.

The leader, who is staying at the Cordis Hotel in Auckland, drew around 80 people last night as he arrived.

Today, he will start with a welcome ceremony and formal bilateral meetings.

Around midday, a live forum is planned to showcase six or seven business sectors “that are of interest to India”, followed by a celebration lunch.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins is also expected to meet Modi in the late afternoon.

Modi’s visit will end with a “massive community event” which thousands of Kiwi Indians are expected to attend at Spark Arena.

One News reported the venue was set to be at capacity, which would be more than 13,000 people.

The Indian leader is then set to depart New Zealand late this evening.

Police operation commander Inspector Grae Anderson this week said additional support from specialist groups was being deployed, including public order teams from across the country.

“These specialist resources will be able to assist with supporter crowds or any other disruptions that may occur.”

Anderson said, given the stature of the visit, the public should expect some disruptions to parts of the city.

Global Risk Consulting Group managing director Chris Kumeroa said authorities kept public security plans broad, so people weren’t able to search for “vulnerabilities”.

The former NZSAS trooper said they could also use a “show of force” to demonstrate a physical security presence and manage risks.

Destiny Church leader Brian Tamaki made incendiary social media comments last month, accusing Modi of targeting Indian Christians with threats and violence.

He later called for “Modi’s visit to be banned and for the India-NZ FTA to be torpedoed”.

“I think we should reciprocate in kind. Let’s purge New Zealand of Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims,” Tamaki said.

“And, while we’re at it, if they’re burning churches down, why don’t we burn mosques and their temples down? Tit for tat.”

Tamaki was served a “temporary firearms licence suspension notice” last month by police and had several hunting weapons confiscated.

The police operation at Tamaki’s home followed his reference on a podcast to using a shotgun to protect his family from immigrants.

Tamaki told the Herald he was speaking figuratively.

After the seizure by police, Tamaki claimed his guns were taken because the Government and police were “bending over backwards” before Modi’s visit.

In a Facebook post, Tamaki accused the police and the Government of “taking my guns to please Modi” after an official notice from the Firearms Safety Authority on his temporary gun suspension.

Inside the Ngongotahā hatchery sustaining Rotorua’s prized trout fisheries

New Zealand Herald July 10, 2026

Eastern Region Fish and Game hatchery manager Mark Sherburn (left) and Eastern Region Fish and Game Hatchery chief executive Arash Alaeinia. Photo / Catherine Fry

Tucked within 10ha of native bush and exotic plantings in Ngongotahā, Fish & Game New Zealand’s Eastern Region headquarters has been a cornerstone of freshwater management since 1937.

Originally established under the New Zealand Wildlife Service, the site today operates as part of Fish & Game NZ, a public entity created under the Conservation Act 1987.

While it reports to the Minister of Conservation, it is not taxpayer-funded, relying largely on revenue from fishing and game bird hunting licences.

One of its key responsibilities is maintaining healthy fish stocks through regulation and restocking.

In the Eastern Region, that work centres on breeding trout for release into Rotorua’s lakes – a task that blends science, precision and a strong connection to New Zealand’s angling heritage.

Trout are not native to New Zealand.

Brown trout were first introduced in the 1860s, after early pioneers overcame the challenge of transporting temperature-sensitive eggs across equatorial seas.

Rainbow trout followed in the 1880s, and both species are now firmly embedded in the country’s freshwater ecosystems.

At Ngongotahā, hatchery manager Mark Sherburn oversees the breeding programme that helps sustain these populations.

“Our hatchery style is a flow-through system,” he said.

“Fresh spring water from the aquifer under the mountain passes through each tank before flowing into the Ngongotahā Stream and on to Lake Rotorua.

“It’s ideal for raising trout.”

The hatchery predominantly works with brown and rainbow trout, although hybrid tiger trout – a rarer cross – are also found in the region, particularly in Lake Rotoiti.

Each year, from April through to the end of August, wild broodstock are collected from Lake Tarawera using a fish trap.

Carefully selected males and females are brought back to the hatchery, where the breeding process begins.

Females are chosen for their size and strong genetics.

When ready, they are anaesthetised and their eggs – or ova – are gently expressed into a container.

Males are then stripped of milt, which is added to fertilise the eggs.

“The milt and eggs are swirled in cold water to create a vortex,” Sherburn explained.

“It mimics what happens in the wild. Fertilisation is immediate.”

Once the process is complete, the adult fish are returned unharmed to their home lakes.

Strict biosecurity measures are followed throughout.

Broodstock are kept separate from hatchery-raised fish, and all equipment is subject to rigorous cleaning protocols to minimise disease risk.

The fertilised eggs are transferred into incubator trays, where they rest on gauze in cool, flowing spring water.

Dim lighting mimics natural river conditions, where eggs would typically be buried beneath gravel.

Within a matter of weeks, tiny black dots – the developing eyes – become visible inside the bright orange ova.

Non-viable eggs are removed to protect the health of the rest.

After about a month, the eggs hatch into alevins – small, tadpole-like fish still sustained by their yolk sacs.

These are kept in dark troughs until they begin to swim freely and seek food.

“That’s when we know they’re ready to move on,” Sherburn said.

From there, the young trout are fed a high-protein diet of commercial salmon feed.

As they grow, they are moved through progressively larger tanks and ponds, mimicking the transition from sheltered streams to open water.

At around 6 months old, the fish are transferred to outdoor ponds.

By the time they reach 1 year, they are ready for release into regional lakes.

While some lakes, such as Lake Rotorua and Lake Tikitapu (Blue Lake), sustain their own trout populations, many others lack suitable spawning habitats.

The hatchery plays a vital role in supplementing these fisheries, ensuring ongoing opportunities for recreational anglers.

Beyond fish production, the site also serves an educational and community function.

The hatchery is open to the public on weekdays, and guided tours are available by arrangement.

During spring, the popular Children’s Fish-Out Days offer young people the chance to catch their own trout.

“For a small donation, we teach them how to fish and catching a trout is guaranteed,” Sherburn said.

“It’s a great way to get kids off screens and outdoors, and to show them where their food comes from.”

With support from the Rotorua Anglers’ Association, fish are filleted on-site, giving children a tangible connection to the process from water to plate.

As pressures on freshwater ecosystems continue to grow, the role of facilities like the Ngongotahā hatchery is increasingly important.

Combining decades of expertise with a deep respect for the environment, the team works quietly behind the scenes to ensure Rotorua’s lakes remain productive and accessible.

For anglers, it means the chance to cast a line into well-stocked waters. For the region, it represents a longstanding commitment to conservation, recreation and community.

Fully furnished house offered as part of job in bid to attract dentist to Wairoa

New Zealand Herald July 10, 2026

The Mene Mai Ano mobile dental clinic in Wairoa is on site, but still needs to be permanently staffed. Photo / Breanna Gower

Wairoa’s mobile oral health unit is giving adults a chance to get their teeth fixed – now it needs a dentist to move to town to take it to the next level.

A full-time job for a two-chair dental clinic serving those aged 18 or older has been advertised in the town for over six months, Kahungunu Executive general manager Sarah Paku said.

“It’s got to be a special person who would want to come to a little town like Wairoa - it’s rural, it’s high needs.”

Paku said the job came with a fully furnished house.

“We try and look after our staff if we can and then hopefully people will say ‘hey I might want to come and work for you’.”

A dental kaiarahi to provide chair-side assistance to the Mene Mai Ano clinical team is also been advertised, with a deadline of July 17.

Paku hopes to be able to hire two dentists, as the unit has the capacity to operate with either two dentists or a dentist and an oral health hygienist concurrently.

The service operates as part of an integrated model, with the workforce shared across fixed and mobile oral health services.

It is currently open Fridays and Saturdays, and will be shut for the Matariki long weekend.

Services include health assessments, basic restorative work, and referral to fixed clinics or secondary services where more complex care is required.

Paku said employing dentists had been “very hard to do”.

“We have had a couple of people interested, but they have gone elsewhere.”

She said the need for people to train elsewhere also added to the struggle.

“They don’t see it as a permanent place; it might be a stepping stone, they might come to Wairoa to work, and they might work themselves up, and then they move on to other places.”

She believed a potential future solution was homegrown.

“If you whakapapa to Wairoa, then it’s easier to place those people.

“Quite a few people are coming back to Wairoa that were brought up here; they have gone away, and some are coming back.”

The town has been without a permanent adult dental service since 2020.

At an initiative called Tō Waha in January to provide free dental care, Golden Apple dentist Isha Woodhams said they were overwhelmed at the number of people needing urgent help.

“I originally thought just three or four days would be enough, and now I think even if I am here for the rest of the year, we might not catch up,” Woodhams said at the time.

Health NZ’s acting general manager of specialist and community services in Hawke’s Bay, Wietske Cloo, said Hawke’s Bay was one of the districts prioritised for investment in the first tranche of the Budget 2022 mobile dental initiative.

“Since 2023, Kahungunu Executive has been working closely with Health New Zealand Hawke’s Bay to deliver a short-term solution to Wairoa’s lack of oral health services.”

Cloo said the units’ placement reduced the cost and time barriers to a population otherwise required to access oral healthcare further away.

“Mene Mai Anō is currently operating the Mobile Oral Health Unit using locum dentists and oral health hygienists who hold contracts with Health New Zealand.

“Locum clinicians are operating the service on Fridays and Saturdays, with ongoing conversations underway about the potential to extend their availability.”

Cloo said there was a shortage of dentists and oral health therapists across the sector.

“This means recruitment of oral health workforce is a challenge for new services such as this one, and particularly in rural communities.”

Michaela Gower joined Hawke’s Bay Today in 2023 and is based out of the Hastings newsroom. She covers Dannevirke and Hawke’s Bay news and loves sharing stories about farming and rural communities.

Letters to the Editor: Dismay at declining defence capabilities, school lunches, solar loan policy

New Zealand Herald July 10, 2026

A Royal New Zealand Air Force P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft overflies HMNZS Aotearoa during surveillance and deterrence activities. Photo / NZDF

Decline in defence

As a former New Zealand Army officer, I’ve watched with dismay as our defence capability has been allowed to wither through decades of chronic underinvestment and political neglect.

Successive governments of all political persuasions have treated defence as a discretionary expense rather than one of the fundamental responsibilities of the state. The result is a force that increasingly resembles a civil defence organisation rather than a credible military.

Our land forces are small and lack depth. Our maritime capability has been steadily eroded. The loss of HMNZS Manawanui – ironically a specialist hydrographic and dive support vessel equipped to survey the seabed – was a sobering reminder that capability, training and operational readiness all matter.

The Royal New Zealand Air Force has also evolved into an organisation with little true combat capability. The retirement of our fighter wing over two decades ago fundamentally changed its role. Today’s Air Force performs valuable air mobility and maritime surveillance tasks, but it is difficult to describe it as an independent fighting force in the traditional sense.

Perhaps it is time to rethink our entire defence force structure. Maritime surveillance assets such as the P-8A Poseidon fleet could logically sit within the Navy, while tactical transport helicopters and Hercules aircraft could be assigned to the Army to directly support land operations.

Such an approach could reduce duplication, streamline headquarters functions and ensure resources are directed to operational capability rather than administration.

The men and women of the New Zealand Defence Force continue to serve with professionalism and dedication. They deserve better than outdated equipment, shrinking capability and governments unwilling to invest in the nation’s security.

The world is becoming less stable, not more. New Zealand can no longer afford to pretend that geography alone is a defence policy.

Champak Mehta, Remuera.

Costs and benefits

It seems to me that Chris Bishop and his colleagues have an extremely narrow idea of how to assess the benefits and costs of their decisions. The dire consequences of his attack on public housing is costing us all, with soaring homelessness and its tragic consequences.

The plan for roads of national significance is just the most recent example. At the same time that our regional roads are rendered impassible, he wants to spend billions of public funds on extending our high-speed highways. It’s also becoming apparent that he expects the rates-capped local councils to repair their own flood damage. Currently that applies to a significant part of the eastern side of both islands.

I’m sure most of the thousands of people currently surveying the devastation of local floods couldn’t care less about roads of national significance. They need a government that will help them repair the damage and help them mitigate the next disaster, maybe even prevent it. It’s called planned resilience and retreat. That’s what we should be focusing on, as our environment is being ravaged on a regular basis.

It’s all a matter of priorities – our current leaders appear to be acting at the behest of lobbyists, not the public.

It’s time for a new set of values, based on the common good, where we can all benefit. Not just those who use their wealth to influence Government ministers for private gain.

Vivien Fergusson, Mt Eden.

Energy issues

As New Zealand heads to a crisis of energy supply and price, there has been little or no incentive put in place this term by the coalition Government to make solar energy more attractive to property owners.

Apart from a half-hearted solar policy proposal by the Labour Party, you would think fossil fuels are here to stay. The power gentailers and retailers have no incentive to encourage solar use as they can’t sell us power that we generate but would prefer to build expensive new generation paid for by us so they can maintain their exorbitant profits.

Our energy future looks bleak without a complete rethink and major reforms.

Graham Fleetwood, Bethlehem.

Pricey imprisonment

It costs a lot of money to keep somebody in prison, so this is very expensive policy (three strikes regime for burglary) for the Act Party to campaign on (July 8).

It’s true that not everybody can be rehabilitated, but surely an attempt to rehabilitate will be more cost-effective and better in terms of social cohesion than throwing everyone in prison to become hardened criminals.

A hardened criminal will spend many years living in prison on the taxpayer’s money.

We don’t want long-term, so-called “dole-bludgers”, so why is there a policy to support long-term “offenders” without first trying interventions?

Mary-Ann de Kort, Gisborne.

Solar loan drawbacks

National and Labour are both trumpeting solar policies (July 9) with the intention of lowering electricity costs for consumers. Unfortunately, there are drawbacks.

A low-interest loan is good in principle, but many families living paycheque to paycheque will be unable to service this loan, either due to poor credit ratings or the inability to take on extra debt now, even though long term there will be savings.

Loans secured against the property (through council rates) rather than the individual would make those properties less desirable on resale, as any new owner would be inheriting the debt.

Maxine Samson, Whakatāne.

No such thing as a fact-free lunch

I would have expected Jonathan Ayling to seek facts before forming opinions.

His assertion that the strongest societies are not those where the Government does most is simply false.

All five Nordic countries are consistently in the top 10 in the world on the happiness scale, based on data from 140 countries.

Finland has been number one for seven years. All are among the highest taxed globally and all provide child benefits, parental leave, health services, hospitals and care for the sick and elderly, paid for by the Government.

Their emphasis is on the wellbeing of the entire population, with high levels of social support and generosity.

This evidence indicates that strong societies come from making sure everyone’s needs are met, not just those who have the nous and the money, with others ending up homeless and hungry. Those are the facts, Mr Ayling.

Susan Grimsdell, Auckland Central.

Keep it simple

Jonathan Ayling is right when he says even the simplest of lunches reflects parents’ care for their child, something that the state should not try to emulate unless there is hardship, illness or addiction involved.

When did butter chicken or beef stir fry become the norm? A piece of fruit and sandwiches remove the competitive element from the lunchbox brigade and are a quiet reminder of parents’ daily care. A note in the lunchbox can be a special bonus on birthdays.

Coming from a family of five, Mum provided the food but we made our own lunches and soon learned for ourselves that a soft pear or jam sandwiches fared badly after the several-kilometre walk to school.

The more the state does for parents, the more dependent they become. Artificial parenting? One more building block in the nanny state. Whoever thought New Zealand would come to this?

Mary Tallon, Mt Albert.

Happiness and wellbeing

We’re again hearing the old chestnut that you can’t tax your way to prosperity. Maybe. But you can tax your way to happiness and wellbeing. The Scandinavian countries have been proving this for many years.

The Green Party proposal of a 2.5% annual tax on net wealth over $10 million is a tiny start, but a wealth tax needs to be progressive, reaching 50% annual tax on net wealth over $100m.

Such people must be persuaded to redistribute their pile or sell up. Nobody needs such a greedy share of our national wealth, and nobody could ever claim to have earned such extraordinary wealth by fair labour. The Government needs more revenue to build more hospitals.

Jim Carlyle, Te Atatū.

Hearty competition

I read with interest (July 9) about the man who holds a world record for the longest-surviving heart bypass patient. My first bypass surgery was in early 1979. This was done in Greenlane Hospital by Dr Ken Graham.

The question is, do I now hold a world record?

John Whitcombe, Tauranga.

Covid-blame fatigue

I, and I’m sure many others, are wondering when Nicola Willis is actually going to stop blaming post-Covid conditions for inflation. It always reminds me of being a parent and bringing up young children, who, when something bad happens, have a tendency to blame someone else or not admit it might be them.

Fortunately, children grow up and learn to take ownership of their actions.

Hamish Walsh, Devonport.

News of a serious injury to an SAS soldier (July 9) brings home the dangers they face and the commitment they show in the interests of our national defence and security.

We owe them a great deal, and for which, “we salute them”.

Larry Mitchell, Rothesay Bay.

With Cadbury shrinking the size of its blocks, is there really still a glass and a half in every one?

Gary Andrews, Mount Maunganui.

As we come together for Matariki, as part of our celebrations we should present Donald Trump with a symbolic rimu wooden spoon – a gentle reminder that his approach to global issues can feel more like stirring up trouble than a gathering enjoying kai in harmony and peaceful union around the table.

Chris Mann, Auckland.

We need to have some balance in the analysis of inappropriate phone use for children under 16 years of age. To blame the app companies for bullying is missing the point. This problem will only be solved by educating the children using phones and encouraging positive behaviour.

Warwick Ayres, Avondale.

You have to feel sorry for Dave Rennie trying to rebuild the current All Blacks as he only really has one halfback to work with.

This lack of replacement halfbacks will be sorely exposed when they travel to South Africa and have to play nine games in five weeks.

Is there any chance they can get the Goat, Aaron Smith, out of retirement?

Jock Mac Vicar, Hauraki.

Napier Inner Harbour boat home seized by council, fisherman neighbour says move has cost man his ‘sanctuary’

New Zealand Herald July 10, 2026

The Meeanee Quay Pier 1 berth after the removal of the Aurora, which the Napier City Council says is part of ongoing work to bring berths and moorings in the Inner Harbour up to a safe, consistent standard for all berth holders. Photo / Doug Laing

The Napier City Council has defended the removal and seizure of a boat that a young man had made into his home and sanctuary.

The Aurora was removed from the Pier 1 berth in the inner harbour at Meeanee Quay last Friday, then taken to the Napier Sailing Club ramp, put aboard a truck and taken away.

A council spokesperson said removing a vessel was always a last resort, and only happened once other options had been exhausted.

“This is part of ongoing work to bring berths and moorings in the Inner Harbour up to a safe, consistent standard for all berth holders,” they said.

The council was “not in a position to comment on individual ownership claims or occupancy arrangements”, but they said it followed “repeated attempts to contact the registered owner, and an abandoned vessel notice that expired without response”.

Friends of the man say he had bought the boat for $500 about a year ago as an abandoned vessel, from the previous owner, who “possibly” had never registered ownership of the boat.

While used as a permanent home moored at the pier, it was seaworthy, said mooring neighbour and career commercial fisherman Karl Warr.

With the man who did not want to be named present, he told Hawke’s Bay Today the young man had had a troubled life, and the mooring was his “safe place - a sanctuary away from negative influences”.

“He’s better off here while he sorts himself out, but they’ve taken away his home,” Warr said.

“He is safe here. As far as I’m aware, no one from the berths here has had any problem.”

He said the council had denied the man a licence to occupy the boat, because it would not recognise him as the owner, and thus would not accept berthage fees the man wanted to pay.

The council says its process draws on multiple sources to establish ownership.

“For recreational vessels, owners are required to provide valid legal proof of ownership,” the spokesperson said.

“Acceptable proof can include insurance documents, slipway or drydock invoices, or sales documentation [where purchased through a commercial entity].

“Under the Inner Harbour Rules and Regulations, Council must be notified of any change of ownership, sale, or change in circumstances relating to a vessel. A new Licence to Occupy is not automatically granted in these situations.”

At Meeanee Quay Piers 1 and 2, there are a total of 41 berths (18 at Pier 1), plus three pole moorings.

Across the water at Jull Wharf in the Iron Pot, where a new pontoon and poles have been installed after closure of the wharf and the moorings at Nelson Quay, there are 20 berths.

Meanwhile, the council is finalising contractor negotiations for “deconstruction” of the Wave Wall at the Nelson Quay entrance to the Iron Pot.

The spokesperson said the council is not yet in a position to confirm specific details such as timing, methodology, or the contractors involved.

“The council is bundling the deconstruction of the Wave Wall and the Discharge Wharf, as both structures are at the end of their operational life,” they said.

The Discharge Wharf has been closed to the public for nearly two years, and an exclusion zone remains in place around the Wave Wall for public safety.

They said removal of the structures is part of the wider Inner Harbour Make Safe programme, and will also enable the council to look at relocating vessels from other areas of the harbour once deconstruction is complete.

Doug Laing is a Hawke’s Bay Today reporter, based in Napier, with more than 50 years’ experience in the news industry. Since joining eventual newspapers merger partner the Daily Telegraph in 1987 he has covered news events and issues throughout Hawke’s Bay.
